newsitem.title: UK: Mark on hold as France concedes missing EMU target.
newsitem.headline: Mark on hold as France concedes missing EMU target.

text.p: An official admission by France that it could not meet the budget deficit-to-GDP ratio required for European monetary union failed to shake the currency market, with the mark barely twitching against European counterparts.

The market had long been expecting France to miss the three percent deficit-to-GDP target -- a crucial standard for membership in monetary union -- considering it only a matter of time before this became public, analysts said.
"The market's been pricing in a budget deficit overshoot by France for some time," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell here.
"There hasn't been much reaction in the markets in that the comment was really nothing new, it's just that it was a bit more explicit than those in the past," Lewis said.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, speaking on Thursday after European markets had finished trading for the day, said the nation's public deficit in 1997 would be more than three percent of GDP.
But Strauss-Kahn hastened to add that Paris was committed to joining the single EMU on time in 1999 and that the government had no intention of letting the deficit run out of control.
Europe's currency market appeared unfazed by Strauss-Kahn's admission on Friday morning, with the mark gaining only slightly on the lira and moving even less on the other European crosses.
The mark was at 3.3735/40 French francs at 0835 GMT compared with the 3.3737/42 seen in late European trade on Thursday. Against the lira, it was at 979.05/25 against 977.15/35.

Now that France had gone on record as saying it could not hit the target, the next point at issue for the market was by how much France would miss the three-percent mark and what action it would take to remedy the situation, analysts said.

"The issue for France is whether they take any policy decisions between now and the budget which would make the fiscal situation worse than it would otherwise be," said Stephen Yorke, director of forex research at SBC Warburg.
Concerning the extent of the overshoot, Strauss-Kahn did not elaborate but only said the ratio would not be three or 3.1.
French daily Liberation on Friday quoted a senior French official as saying Paris was aiming for a deficit/GDP ratio of 3.3 percent in 1997 and to cut this to three percent in 1998.

"If it looks like they are going to be closer to 3.7 percent, it could throw in doubt the whole idea of EMU going ahead on time, because the Germans wouldn't see that as acceptable," said Juli Collins-Thompson, economist at Yamaichi International here.
"But if it looks like they're going to overshoot only moderately, that should be good for the peripheral European markets, which is where the key lies in all of this," she said.

Much of the market's perception on whether monetary union will include only model pupils who meet the criteria or be more broad-based has centred on whether "core" EMU candidates like Germany and France can fulfill the conditions.

If the core nations themselves cannot make the grade, the market perceives they would have no excuse to exclude the "peripheral" nations like Italy, Spain and Portugal if they themselves missed the targets by modest amounts.
France's confession preceded a flood of comments from top German officials, none of which mentioned France by name.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the euro would be launched on time in 1999 and in line with the criteria which will not be changed.

Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said it would be wrong to consider there was too much leeway on the three-percent figure. Fellow member Reimut Jochimsen said the EMU stability pact, designed to ensure fiscal discipline after 1999, was at risk from "less stability-minded" nations.
The reaction, analysts said, did not signal any change in the EMU timetable or the chances of France qualifying, as long as Paris's fiscal state does not worsen this year.

"That (not worsening public finances) would allow for a downward trend from 1996 to 1997, and provided that the 1998 numbers show a further improvement, there is no reason why EMU should not start on time," SBC Warburg's Yorke said.
